title: Penrose diary — 12 March 1932
---

12 March 1932. Baisha Island.

The tower stands at last. Forty-one feet of whitewashed stone on the south cliff, and the lantern glass arrived from Birmingham on Tuesday's junk without a single crack. I, Arthur Penrose, engineer to the Harbour Office, may now say that the Baisha light is built, nine months after the first stone was laid.

Beneath the cliff the masons broke into a natural cave while cutting the landing stair. Rather than fill it, I have had it squared into a small stone room with an iron door, to serve as a store for lamp oil. It was a poor idea: the sea fills it twice a day, and the fishermen already call it the tide room.

I ordered a brass key cast for the iron door, about the length of a man's hand, and asked the smith in the harbour to engrave two Chinese characters on its bow, 潮汐, meaning tide, so that no keeper would confuse it with the key to the tower. The first keeper, a quiet fisherman named Chou, will hold it, and he is to pass it to whoever keeps the light after him.

Tomorrow I begin teaching Chou to trim the wick and wind the clockwork that turns the lens.
